summary: Enables more students to undertake recognised experiential and interdisciplinary learning beyond the boundaries of their course through shared institutional pathways, with Year 1 focused on sandwich-year reform and validation of a shared 15-credit Level 6 experiential-learning capstone.
detailSummary:
Near-curriculum describes learning beyond the core disciplinary course that is formally docked with a student's degree through credit or official institutional recognition. It creates legitimate space within the study pathway for students to work across disciplines, engage with external audiences and integrate meaningful experience into their education. Attaching credit or recognition signals that these experiences matter and improves access for students who have less capacity to undertake additional extracurricular activity.

King's will establish shared academic, regulatory and administrative structures that programmes can adopt without creating bespoke provision or redesigning their disciplinary core. These will include the smallest viable suite of adaptable optional 15-credit modules, supporting interdisciplinary and vertical projects, work with external audiences, cross-disciplinary themes such as entrepreneurship, and a reflective route through which accumulated experiential learning can be synthesised and recognised for credit.

The first mobilisation priority is deliberately concrete. From September 2026 to approximately April 2027, King's will develop and ratify a new institutional policy and regulatory model for sandwich years, making them easier for programmes to offer and students to access without each programme constructing a separate route. In parallel, King's will design and validate a shared 15-credit Level 6 experiential-learning capstone or wrapper module through which students can bring together accumulated experiential learning using structured reflection, synthesis and assessment.

These two products will act as practical tests of the wider near-curriculum proposition. Learning from their policy, approval, administration, timetabling, recognition and student-experience requirements will be used to identify the next reusable routes worth developing. Sequencing beyond those early products will remain deliberately evidence-led rather than committing in advance to a large suite of shared modules.

The deliverable will also establish the governance and assurance routes required by other elements of King's Edge where formal credit or recognition is needed. Their substantive propositions remain with the relevant deliverables. Deliverable 2.2.2 provides the shared partnership and operational infrastructure where externally engaged opportunity is required; 2.2.3 owns the academic, regulatory and administrative pathways through which learning becomes formal provision.

caseForChange.problem:
University has traditionally given students space to explore who they might become. Through their course and the wider university experience, students test possible futures, build confidence, develop relationships and gain experience. For some, these ambitions align closely with their discipline. For others, the future they begin to create sits alongside, crosses or departs substantially from the subject they study.

The graduate premium therefore extends beyond the learning outcomes of a course. It also emerges through the choices students make, the contexts they encounter and the opportunities they have to apply and extend their learning. Universities have relied heavily on extracurricular activity to carry this wider development, requiring students to find additional time around their formal studies and creating particular barriers for those with work, caring responsibilities or other demands.

Opportunities that cross disciplines, programmes or faculties are also difficult to create from a single academic base. Current sandwich-year routes and credit-bearing provision can require bespoke programme-level policy, approval and administration, creating friction that limits access and makes institution-wide growth difficult.
caseForChange.opportunity:
King's can establish near-curriculum learning as a recognised part of the formal degree, giving students dedicated space, credit or official recognition to pursue ambition-aligned learning beyond their course. A deliberately small number of shared module shells, regulatory routes and administrative models can support varied provision without requiring every programme to create bespoke structures.

The immediate opportunity is to prove this through two concrete institutional products: a reusable sandwich-year policy and regulatory model, and a shared 15-credit Level 6 experiential-learning capstone or wrapper module. Together they provide practical evidence about the academic, regulatory and administrative architecture needed for later near-curriculum growth.
caseForChange.whyNow: Current work on the Curriculum Framework, experiential learning, skills recognition and wider King's Edge provision creates a live window to establish common near-curriculum architecture before separate regulatory and administrative routes proliferate. Sandwich-year reform and the shared experiential-learning capstone are sufficiently concrete to progress now and can generate implementation learning while the broader North Star and curriculum-growth picture mature.
caseForChange.intendedChange: King's establishes reusable academic, regulatory and administrative pathways through which students can undertake formally recognised learning beyond their disciplinary core. In Year 1 the University ratifies a clearer sandwich-year model and validates a shared 15-credit Level 6 experiential-learning capstone, then uses those products to identify the next institutional routes worth developing. Over the following mobilisation years, the architecture is tested and extended selectively in response to demand, curriculum priorities and evidence.

problemSolved: King's lacks sufficiently simple and reusable institutional routes through which programmes can create formal space, credit or recognition for learning beyond the disciplinary core without building bespoke policy, modules and administration each time.
whatChanges: King's establishes shared near-curriculum pathways, beginning with sandwich-year reform and a validated Level 6 experiential-learning capstone, then extends the architecture selectively where evidence shows that common routes will improve access, quality and efficiency.
